blocks.text: 1. Vector Updates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301794-280934609.png
Vector Updates closes the gap between a static one time load and a living collection: it covers how existing vectors get modified after initial ingestion.
It replaces an already stored vector's content once its underlying source document changes, an ongoing maintenance operation every production collection needs.
2. Source Content Never Stays Still
As covered in Document Ingestion, an updated source document needs its stored vector updated too.
The vector database has to support changing an already indexed entry, not just adding new ones.
3. Vectors Aren't Easy To Edit In Place

blocks.alt: Vectors Aren't Easy To Edit In Place
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301794-445780470.png
An index organizes vectors based on their position at the time it was built, as covered in Indexing.
Simply overwriting a vector's numbers can leave the surrounding index structure inconsistent.
4. Delete And Reinsert Pattern
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301794-33920793.png
Many vector databases handle an update as removing the old vector and inserting the new one.
That two step pattern keeps the index internally consistent without needing special case logic.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Update approach","Index impact"],"rows":[["Direct overwrite","Risks leaving index structure inconsistent"],["Delete and reinsert","Keeps index structure consistent using existing logic"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Re-Embedding Trigger Points
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301794-402034892.png
A changed chunk needs a fresh embedding computed before it can replace the old vector.
The update pipeline has to trigger both re-chunking and re-embedding together.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Updating a document's stored vector without first re-running it through chunking and embedding leaves the database holding a vector that no longer accurately represents the actual current content.

blocks.text: 6. Update Consistency Across Replicas
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301794-268774648.png
An update needs to propagate to every replica, not just one, as covered in Replication.
A lagging replica can briefly return the old vector after an update has already happened elsewhere.
7. Batch Updates Versus Single Updates
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447301795-492937369.png
Updating vectors one at a time works fine at small scale, but becomes slow across many changes.
Batching many updates together reduces overhead compared to many individual operations.
8. Update Frequency And Index Health
Frequent updates can degrade an index's structure over time, a concern already raised around rebuilding after large changes in Indexing.
Periodic rebuilding stays relevant even for update heavy collections.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Robust Vector Update Support Matters Most

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Robust Vector Update Support Matters Most
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447302299-412500301.png
Frequently changing source content needs reliable vector updates.
Static, rarely changing content rarely exercises the update path at all.
10. Worked Example
The example below applies the delete and reinsert update pattern to a changed document.

code.content:
vector_store = {
    "doc_1": {"vector": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3], "text": "Original refund policy text."},
    "doc_2": {"vector": [0.5, 0.1, 0.4], "text": "Shipping timeline details."},
}

def fake_embed(text):
    # a stand-in for a real embedding model call
    return [round(len(text) / 100, 3), round(text.count("a") / 10, 3), 0.0]

def update_vector(vector_store, doc_id, new_text):
    # delete the old vector, then re-embed and insert the new one
    if doc_id in vector_store:
        del vector_store[doc_id]
        print(f"  Deleted old vector for {doc_id}")
    new_vector = fake_embed(new_text)
    vector_store[doc_id] = {"vector": new_vector, "text": new_text}
    print(f"  Inserted new vector for {doc_id}: {new_vector}")

print("Before update:")
print(f"  {vector_store['doc_1']}")

print("\nUpdating doc_1 with revised policy text:")
update_vector(vector_store, "doc_1", "Updated refund policy allows returns within sixty days.")

print("\nAfter update:")
print(f"  {vector_store['doc_1']}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the old vector removed before the freshly re-embedded new vector takes its place, ensuring the stored data always reflects the current source content.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Overwriting a vector's raw values directly instead of using a delete and reinsert pattern.
Updating a document's stored vector without first re-running chunking and embedding on the new text.
Assuming an update instantly reaches every replica instead of accounting for propagation delay.
Never rebuilding the index despite a high volume of frequent vector updates over time.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Vector updates replace an already stored vector's content when its source document changes.
An updated source document needs its stored vector updated, not just newly ingested documents.
An index organizes vectors by position, so overwriting risks leaving that structure inconsistent.
Many vector databases handle updates as deleting the old vector and inserting a new one.
A changed chunk needs fresh re-chunking and re-embedding before it can replace the old vector.
An update needs to propagate to every replica, and a lagging replica can briefly return stale data.
Batching many updates together reduces overhead compared to many individual operations.
Frequent updates can degrade an index's structure, keeping periodic rebuilding relevant.
